newsitem.title: USA: Ford CEO sees U.S. auto sales staying strong.
newsitem.headline: Ford CEO sees U.S. auto sales staying strong.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. Chairman and Chief Executive Officer Alex Trotman on Wednesday said the mid-summer momentum of U.S. vehicle sales is likely to continue well into August.
Talking to reporters at the University of Michigan annual auto conference, Trotman said he also does not expect the U.S. economy to slip into a recession in 1998, 1999, or 2000.
"It was a very strong industry we saw in July, and I think August may well be another very strong month," said Trotman.

Trotman said Ford has not changed its total vehicle outlook for 1997 in the U.S. from the 15.5 million rate. Light vehicle U.S. sales in July finished the month at about 15.3 million units, based on year-ago seasonal factors from the U.S. Commerce Department, the most recent available.

In his prepared remarks, Trotman warned that an international treaty now under consideration to address global warming concerns could lead to higher energy costs, less affordable vehicles and driving restrictions.

Trotman said there is a "strong possibility" that negotiators from major countries around the world will sign a legally binding international treaty on global warming when they meet in December in Kyoto, Japan.
"If that agreement is made legally binding, there is no doubt in our mind there will be a huge impact on the GDP of the major nations," Trotman told reporters.

"The net effect would be a transfer of jobs and industry with little or no reduction of energy use worldwide. All this to address a problem that may or may not be the result of human activity," he said.

Trotman said the proposed treaty would force the U.S. to roll back carbon dioxide emissions to below 1990 levels by 2010. Developed countries such as the U.S. would make more sacrifices than developing countries such as China, Korea, Brazil and India under the proposed treaty, he said.
Developing countries now account for 50 percent of carbon emissions, and will be responsible for about 75 percent by the end of the next century, according to Trotman.
"Such a treaty could lead to higher energy costs for consumers and businesses, making automobiles and a variety of other products less affordable," Trotman said.
Trotman said world leaders should wait until there is a consensus among the scientific community about the cause of the current warming pattern.
